blocks.x: Dreaming of a Japanese name for your future child? Whether you love the culture or have a Japanese spouse, there are some common Japanese names that might give you some inspiration. Like “John” or “Maria” in English, there are some very popular Japanese names, some of them so common that you encounter them on textbooks! Regardless of that, each one carries a meaning that helps explain its staying power.
So, find out some of the most common names to know in Japanese and how to read them so that when you see them on staff name tags, you’ll know how to address them!
Should I Address Someone by Their First or Last Name?

In Japan, it’s customary to address people outside of your family and friends by their last name, especially when you first meet them. Generally, when you address someone you should respect or don’t know well, use their last name with an honorific suffix, like 〜さん (~san) or 〜さま (~sama). This is especially important in Japanese email, since it’s standard to start by addressing the person’s surname with a suffix.

However, with family, friends, classmates, or close colleagues, you can be more relaxed and drop the formalities. It would come across as cold and unnatural to address someone you know by their surname. It’s more common to use their first name, often with a casual suffix like 〜くん (~kun) or even 〜ちゃん (~chan) to address them in a friendlier and warmer manner.
Most Common Japanese Family Names & Their Origins

There are over 100,000 distinct Japanese surnames, often related to geography, occupation, and nature. A common name, such as 山田 (yamada), means “mountain field,” likely reflecting where the family lived.

Before the Meiji Era, only nobles such as samurai officially carried surnames, often to tie themselves to the land they protected or ruled. However, during the Meiji Restoration, the government required all people, including commoners, to officially register a surname. Many had to choose a name, but only from a limited number of government-approved kanji. So, it was common to choose popular names they heard, which would vary by region. That’s why you’ll find certain surnames are common in some areas and not others.

Married couples are generally required to officially use the same family name (usually the husband’s surname); however, this is actually not a traditional practice. Japan adopted it from the West and stipulated it into policy in 1898. But more companies and government organizations are accepting birth names, and Japanese government officials have raised the possibility of amending the policy multiple times. So, it might not be too surprising to come across Japanese couples with different family names.
List of the Most Common Japanese Surnames

Here is a list of the most common Japanese surnames, ranked by the number of people who carry them. (Note that while these names are the most common, they might not be very common in certain regions; most of the names are very uncommon in Okinawa):
SurnameMeaning/Description

1. 佐藤 (Satou)Satou is the most common surname in Japan, with around 1.99 million people carrying the name as of 2008. The name is particularly popular in Hokkaido, Tohoku, and Kyushu. The name comes from the famous 藤原 (Fujiwara) clan, from which the second kanji character, 藤 (Tou/Fuji), comes.
2. 鈴木 (Suzuki)Suzuki is the most common surname in the Kanto region and the second most common nationwide. The name literally means “bell tree.”
3. 高橋 (Takahashi)The third most common name, and is particularly popular in Tohoku and Shikoku. Takahashi translates somewhat to “tall bridge.”
4. 渡辺 (Watanabe)Watanabe is common throughout Japan, with higher concentrations around the Yamanashi and Shizuoka prefectures as well as Kyushu. However, the name actually originates from Osaka.
5. 田中 (Tanaka)Tanaka is another name you will commonly find across Japan; it is more frequent in Western Japan compared to other areas.

6. 伊藤 (Itou)Itou is common in a variety of Japanese regions, such as the Kanto, Chukyo, and Sannin regions. Nagoya city has the highest number of individuals with the Itou surname. It also shares the same 藤 (tou) kanji as 佐藤 (Satou) and comes from the Fujiwara clan name as well.
7. 山本 (Yamamoto)You’ve probably heard the name Yamamoto before since it’s quite common across northeastern and western Japan. It’s the most frequent name in the Kinki and Sanyo regions.
8. 中村 (Nakamura)Nakamura is also very common throughout Japan, especially in the Western areas.
9. 小林 (Kobayashi)Kobayashi is another very common name found across Japan, especially in Kanto, Shinetsu, Kinki, and Chugoku.
10. 加藤 (Katou)Katou originates from Ishikawa Prefecture and is now most common in the Chugyo region. It also comes from the Fujiwara clan name, as evidenced by its second kanji 藤 (Tou).
Top 15 Most Common Japanese Names

Japanese names are often inspired by many things such as nature or characteristics of the name itself. Many names are chosen based on their kanji meanings, aesthetics, or both. Kanji is actually a rather important aspect of Japanese names since each character can convey a certain meaning or even luck that parents might want to associate with their child.

Similar to English, there are many names that are usually gendered as male or female. But you will also have plenty of unisex names as well. So, let’s dive into the most popular male, female, and unisex names based on a 2025 Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance survey.
Most Common Names for Girls

While Japanese female names vary widely, they often include 子 (ko) at the end, which is thought to give the name a more feminine appeal. So, common names like 花 (hana) might include 子 to make 花子 (Hanako). In this list, we include many names that often have 子 at the end but for the sake of simplicity, we mostly left it out.
1. 翠 (Sui/Midori)

翠 (Midori) is the most popular female name, and it actually topped the list for the first time in 2025. The name translates to “kingfisher” and makes up part of the word for “jade,” which in Japanese is 翡翠 (Hisui). Jade is considered to bring good fortune and conveys wishes for a happy and beautiful life.
2. 陽葵 (Himari)
陽葵 (Himari) takes second place as the most common name for Japanese girls. It is associated with the cheerfulness of the sun and sunflowers.
3. 紬 (Tsumugi)
紬 (Tsumugi), named for a type of woven silk fabric. So, it’s a popular name for girls for its popular associations with craftsmanship and patience.
4. ましろ Mashiro
茉白 (Mashiro) is another common name with a very pretty meaning, combining jasmine, 茉 (ma), and white, 白 (shiro), so “white jasmine.” So, it’s no surprise it’s a popular name for girls in Japan.
5. 凛 (Rin)
凛 (Rin) is actually a gender-neutral name, but it’s especially common with females compared to males. It actually translates to “dignified and poised.”
6. 陽菜 (Hina)
陽菜 (Hina) pairs the kanji for “sun” with the kanji for “greens” or “vegetables,” giving an image of something nurtured and warmed by sunlight.
7. Ema

If you consider the most popular name by reading rather than specific kanji, Ema ranks as the most popular name overall. So, this name might not have one singular meaning since it can consist of different kanji.
Wondering how to say your name in Japanese? Check out our blog: What Is My Name in Japanese? Japanese Name Generator
Most Popular Male Names

Boy names also vary widely and sometimes are based on naming traditions like the order of who was born first: 陽一 (Yoichi), meaning first son, and 真二 (Shinji), meaning second son. Like female names, many are chosen for their meaning, sound, and aesthetic.
8. 湊 (Minato/Sou)

湊 (Minato) means “harbor” or “a place where water gathers,” and topped the boys’ list for the first time in 2025. It expresses parents’ hopes that their child will be sociable and have many meaningful encounters with others.
9. 伊織 (Iori)
伊織 combines kanji without a strong standalone meaning on their own, but together they carry an elegant, literary feel often associated with building connections.
10. 結翔 (Yuito/Yuuto)
結翔 (Yuito) pairs “to connect” with “to soar,” blending the idea of relationships with ambition.
11. 琉生 (Rui/Ruki)
琉生 (Rui) uses the kanji for “lapis lazuli” or “gem” alongside “life” or “born,” giving the name a precious, vibrant image.
12. 蓮 (Ren)
蓮 (Ren) means “lotus,” a flower strongly associated with purity and resilience in Japanese and Buddhist symbolism.
13. 朔 (Saku)
朔 (Saku) refers to the “new moon,” giving the name a quiet, fresh-start kind of meaning.
Most Popular Unisex Japanese Names
Gender-neutral naming has become an increasingly visible trend in Japan, with parents choosing names that work equally well for boys or girls.
14. せな (Sena)
Sena topped the gender-neutral name rankings in 2025. It’s typically written in hiragana or with kanji chosen more for sound than fixed meaning, which is common among genderless names.
15. 葵 (Aoi)
葵 (Aoi) means “hollyhock,” a flowering plant, and has remained one of the most enduring unisex names in Japan for years.
16. 陽向/陽太 (Hinata)

Hinata, meaning “sunny place” or “facing the sun,” is one of the most well-established gender-neutral names, regularly appearing near the top of both boys’ and girls’ rankings depending on the kanji used.
Conclusion: The Most Common Japanese Names are Full of Meaning!

Japanese names and surnames have a long history and can carry significant meanings. While historically, many commoners didn’t officially have last names, today they are very important, especially since it’s a standard for Japanese etiquette to address people by their surname. However, with close friends, family, and even colleagues, you can use their first name! You’ll probably meet at least a few people who have the names from this list!

FAQ:
What is the most common Japanese name?

It depends on how you count it. By kanji, 湊 (Minato) and 翠 (Sui) topped the boys’ and girls’ rankings in 2025, but by reading alone, Haruto has been the single most popular boys’ name for 17 years running, since many different kanji combinations can all be read as “Haruto.”
Why do so many Japanese names have multiple readings?
The same kanji can often be pronounced several different ways depending on the parents’ choice, which is why names like 陽翔 can be read as Haruto, Hinato, or Haruka.
Why do many Japanese female names end in 子 (ko)?
子 is traditionally added to make a name sound more feminine, though it’s been less common in recent naming trends compared to its peak popularity decades ago.
What's a "genderless" or unisex name in Japan?
These are names chosen to work for either gender, often written in hiragana or with kanji selected more for their sound than a fixed masculine or feminine meaning, like Sena, Aoi, or Hinata.
